articles.title: Centre authorises states, UTs to exercise powers under UAPA against Zakir Naik’s IRF
articles.text:
Centre authorises states, UTs to exercise powers under UAPA against Zakir Naik’s IRF
New Delhi, The Centre has authorised states and Union territories to exercise powers related to funds and premises under the stringent Unlawful Activities Act, 1967, in relation to fugitive preacher Zakir Naik's Islamic Research Foundation , which was declared an unlawful association earlier this month.
In a gazette notification issued on Thursday, the Ministry of Home Affairs invoked powers under Section 42 of the anti-terror law to issue the directive to state governments and Union territory administrators.
The ministry had extended the ban on the IRF as an unlawful association through a notification dated November 13 under sections 3 and 3 of the Act.
"The Central government declared the Islamic Research Foundation an unlawful association vide notification number S.O. 6182 dated November 13, 2026, published in the Gazette of India; in exercise of the powers conferred by Section 42 of the Unlawful Activities Act, 1967, the Central government hereby directs that all powers exercisable by it under sections 7 and 8 of the said Act shall also be exercised by the state governments and the Union territory administrations in relation to the above said unlawful association," the notification said.
Section 7 of the UA pertains to the powers of the government to prohibit the use or transfer of funds, securities and other financial assets suspected of being used or intended for the purposes of an unlawful association.
It also allows authorised officers to investigate such financial dealings, whereas Section 8 empowers the government to notify premises, including houses and buildings, suspected of being used for the activities of an unlawful association.
Following the notification, the authorities can regulate access to a premises and restrict the use of movable properties found there.
On November 13, the Centre extended the ban on fugitive preacher Zakir Naik's IRF for another five years under the stringent UA. The ban was to expire on November 14.
Naik, a resident of Maharashtra, was on a trip abroad when the government banned his organisation in 2016. Since then, he has been living in Malaysia. In 2017, his passport was also revoked at the request of the National Investigation Agency , which registered a case against him.
India has been pursuing legal and diplomatic measures against Naik since November 17, 2016, when the Central government declared his organisation an unlawful association citing allegations of promoting enmity and hatred between religious communities.
In May 2017, India approached INTERPOL for a Red Corner Notice against Naik, providing subsequent clarifications in August and October.
However, during its 102nd session in late December 2017, the Interpol Commission deemed the request premature because a charge-sheet had not been filed at the time of the initial application.
Based on a fresh court warrant issued on November 24, 2017, the Indian agencies submitted a renewed RCN request to INTERPOL on January 3, 2018, a response to which remains awaited.
India had also formally transmitted a provisional arrest and extradition request to Malaysia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs on January 19, 2018, after it was confirmed that Naik had been granted permanent residency status.

articles.title: Judicial member must for ED attachment cases: Supreme Court
articles.text:
Utkarsh Anand is the National Legal Editor at Hindustan Times, where he leads the newspaper's coverage of the Supreme Court, constitutional law, the judiciary and the Union law ministry. He joined Hindustan Times in 2020 after stints at Press Trust of India (PTI), The Indian Express and CNN-News18, and has over two decades of experience reporting on law, governance and public policy. His work has focussed on some of India's most consequential constitutional and legal developments, including the Supreme Court's judgments on Article 370, marriage equality, decriminalisation of homosexuality, the Babri Masjid dispute, electoral reforms and judicial appointments. He specialises in making complex legal proceedings and judgments accessible to readers while examining their wider social and political impact. Beyond daily reportage, Utkarsh has led investigative projects and enterprise reporting that have shaped public debate and prompted institutional responses. His work has received several journalism awards, including the Ramnath Goenka Excellence in Journalism Award. As National Legal Editor, he has also played a key role in expanding Hindustan Times' legal journalism footprint, mentoring reporters and strengthening coverage across platforms. A Chevening South Asia Journalism Programme Fellow, Utkarsh regularly writes analyses on the judiciary and constitutional issues, and his reporting is widely followed by lawyers, judges, policymakers, academics and readers seeking clarity on India's evolving legal landscape.
Judicial member must for ED attachment cases: Supreme Court
The court held that such consequential decisions cannot be left to a member without a legal background.
The Supreme Court on Thursday ruled that the adjudicating authority (AA) under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) must include a judicial member while deciding whether to confirm the Enforcement Directorate’s (ED) provisional attachment of properties, holding that such consequential decisions cannot be left to a member without a legal background.
A bench, comprising Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, clarified that while a single-member bench can undertake adjudication under the law, it must necessarily comprise the judicial member of the AA. The requirement, the court said, flows from the need to ensure legal objectivity when determining whether properties are involved in money laundering, a finding that can have serious consequences for the rights of individuals.
The ruling settles an important legal question that had divided high courts, with the Delhi, Calcutta and Telangana high courts having declined to insist on the presence of a judicial member in every bench of the AA. The Supreme Court has now drawn a clear distinction between the authority’s administrative and adjudicatory functions, holding that the former can be performed without a judicial member but the latter cannot.
“The AA is, however, plainly more than a custodian of records. As its very name indicates, its principal task is ‘adjudication’ under Section 8 of the PMLA,” noted the bench, distinguishing between the authority acting as the “keeper of the sealed cover” and when “it holds the scales”.
The court explained that when the ED provisionally attaches a property, it forwards the order, along with the material relied upon, to the AA, which preserves these records. This custodial function does not involve substantive decision-making or the appreciation of competing submissions and can, therefore, be discharged without a judicial member.
However, the position changes when the AA hears the affected person and the ED, examines the evidence and determines whether the property is involved in money laundering. Such an exercise requires the application of legal principles, interpretation of statutory provisions and appreciation of evidence, it said.
“The application of an independent judicial mind is...adequately ensured by the presence of a Judicial Member in the Bench undertaking adjudication under Sections 8(2) and 8(3) of PMLA,” it held.
The bench also rejected the Centre’s argument that the availability of an appeal before the appellate tribunal and subsequently the high court was sufficient safeguard against any erroneous decision by the AA.
“An appellate forum may correct the errors in a decision; it cannot supply what the original forum lacked,” said the court, adding that a defect in proceedings before the AA on account of the absence of a judicial member cannot be cured merely because an appeal lies to a judicial forum.
It further clarified that a judicial member need not necessarily be appointed as the chairperson of the AA. The chairperson’s role, it said, was essentially administrative, involving the constitution of benches and allocation of cases, and did not require the same application of legal mind as the adjudicatory process.
It accordingly directed the chairperson to issue the necessary administrative circular to ensure that every bench passing an order under Section 8(3) of the PMLA includes a judicial member. The court also extended the requirement to certain consequential determinations under other provisions of the PMLA, which are intrinsically linked to the adjudication of attachment, freezing or retention of property and records.
Notably, the judgment did not invalidate the issuance of show-cause notices under Section 8(1) by a bench without a judicial member, nor did it mandate that every adjudication must be conducted by a bench of two or more members. A single-member bench remains permissible, provided the member is drawn from the field of law.
The bench also clarified that its ruling would not automatically reopen orders already passed by a single, non-judicial member before Thursday. Persons aggrieved by such orders would, however, remain free to challenge them on their merits through the statutory appellate remedy.
SC flags need for multiple adjudicating authorities
Separately, the bench nudged the Centre to reconsider the 2009 amendment to the PMLA that restricted the number of adjudicating authorities to one, recommending that the government examine the desirability of restoring the original framework of multiple AAs, including regional authorities.
Pointing to the steep rise in provisional attachment orders (PAOs), the court said the existing arrangement was placing enormous pressure on the authority, particularly when it was required to complete adjudication within the statutory period of 180 days.
According to figures furnished by the ED, a total of 3,639 PAOs had been issued since July 2005. While 321 such orders were issued in 2023-24, the number rose to 461 in 2024-25 and further jumped to 712 in 2025-26. Another 138 PAOs were issued up to August 31, 2026.
The bench noted that the expansion of offences under the PMLA schedule and the consequent widening of proceedings under the law would only add to the workload, including applications for retention of seized properties and records.
“This juxtaposition of the increasing cases and the time-bound nature of adjudication, to our mind, puts an enormous pressure on the Members of the AA, especially those involved in the process of adjudication,” it said.
The court observed that the 2009 amendment, which replaced the original provision allowing the Centre to appoint one or more adjudicating authorities with a framework providing for only one, appeared to have created “an undesirable, if not unsolvable, lock-jam of cases at the level of the AA”. It cautioned that such circumstances could induce hurried and hasty decisions, adversely affecting stakeholders’ ability to access justice.
The bench said it would ordinarily have exercised its powers under Article 142 of the Constitution to direct the Centre to notify additional adjudicating authorities, which would also enable the creation of regional AAs. However, since the 2009 amendment itself was not under challenge, it refrained from issuing such a direction.
Instead, it recommended that the Union government “appropriately consider the suitability and desirability of repealing the 2009 Amendment and reverting to the original framework of multiple Adjudicating Authorities and take necessary steps for the same”.
In its concluding observations, the bench described the PMLA as a law of “exceptional rigour”, stressing that its stringent provisions must be accompanied by safeguards at the stage when an affected person gets the opportunity to contest the attachment of property.
“Independence of position is, however, only one half of that assurance. Where the authority is called upon to weigh evidence, apply statutory presumptions and construe the law, the assurance is fully honoured only when the person who decides is trained in the discipline of the law,” it said.

HMSI has been the country's second-largest two-wheeler maker since its separation from Hero MotoCorp in 2014, and even outsold its former partner in monthly sales on multiple occasions. Microsoft: Hackers in China, N Korea using ARTEX AI tool to break into global tech systems
articles.text:
Chinese and North Korean state-sponsored hacking crews are among the growing number of groups known for using the ARTEX pentesting tool in attacks, Microsoft said this week.

ARTEX is an open source, AI-powered penetration testing framework that attackers have adopted to automate reconnaissance, credential attacks, and exploitation since its public release in July.

Campaigns that have been linked to ARTEX have targeted cloud environments, IT software like ConnectWise, and financial institutions globally, sometimes reaching privileged access in under three hours.

Salt Typhoon is arguably the most recognizable name on the list of ARTEX beneficiaries – the group responsible for attacks on telcos AT&T and Verizon, US government systems, UK prime minister's aides, and more.

The lesser-known Crystal Typhoon – the group behind the ArcaneDoor attacks back when Microsoft called it Storm-1849 – was also named alongside it, as were North Korea's Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet.

Microsoft also named China-state-aligned Storm-0940, linked to the ConnectWise compromise, and financially motivated, Cambodia-based Storm-3358. It had previously reported both groups' use of ARTEX.

Chinese cybersecurity company ThreatBook claimed ownership of ARTEX in November. GitHub user "Autumn-27" originally published its source code with a Chinese-language interface in July.

Various forks of the repo, which was taken down in October, have meant that the same framework is available in multiple languages.

According to Infrawatch, there are more than 130 variants of ARTEX in circulation, and it is the most widely used agentic offensive framework (AOF) at present.

Like other offensive security tools adopted by criminals, ARTEX can lower the effort required to mount attacks. Experienced groups can also use it to automate repetitive work and pursue multiple avenues at once.

As Microsoft echoed this week, after the FBI and AWS issued their warnings earlier this month, ARTEX is proving to be a useful tool for the more sophisticated groups to streamline and hasten their attacks too.

It's being used to help attackers steal AI and cloud credentials at "industrial scale," as AWS put it, which provide attackers access to advanced models for free.

Microsoft says ARTEX can progress from reconnaissance to persistent, privileged access within minutes, depending on its configuration and the target's defenses.

"In the past few weeks, we've reported several distinct campaigns that abused ARTEX to search public repositories for exposed secrets, enable supply chain compromise, and scan internet-facing systems for exploitation," its threat intelligence team blogged. "These campaigns illustrate how threat actors use ARTEX to automate various stages of the attack chain.

"Threat actors define scope and targets for ARTEX, which then uses AI agents to set verifiable goals, define tactical steps for each stage of the operation, use tools to attack targets, create graphs to track discovered systems and results of actions, and report back to the threat actor."

Notably, ARTEX does not offer any new attack techniques. All of the tool's capabilities were previously known to the cybersecurity world, but its value lies in the automation capabilities it offers users, chaining attacks at machine speed.

In the UK NCSC's warning about AOFs this week, it said the key strengths of this technology are its speed, its thoroughness in probing target systems for weaknesses, how it learns from failures instantly, and that it is inexpensive to run at scale.

AOFs' speed comes at a cost, however. These tools are noisy, the NCSC said, making them easier to detect in network logs and by defensive solutions.

Some examples of the attacks in which the tool has been implicated include Storm-0940's hit on ConnectWise, which enabled attempted sign-ins to more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, various financial institutions in South Korea and India, UK registrar 123 Reg, and the European Commission. ®

articles.title: Indie web browser Ladybird enters alpha testing
articles.text:
The independent Ladybird web browser has reached an important milestone: an alpha test version. What's more, it works well. These may not be the criteria by which some will judge it, though.

Earlier this week, the developer behind the Ladybird web browser announced that Ladybird is now in alpha. We've given it a brief test, and it performed very well. It's more stable and works better than its alpha label would suggest.

There are downloads available, covering macOS on Apple Silicon, as well as for Linux on x86-64; for the latter, there's a Flatpak package, as well as native Ubuntu and Fedora packages.

It's an open source project, so you can download the source code from the GitHub repository and compile it yourself, but in an unusual move, back in June the project announced that the developers would no longer accept public code contributions.

We first mentioned Ladybird as part of our early 2022 look at its original parent project – SerenityOS: Remarkable project with its own JS-capable web browser. Both the name and the date are significant: the former is a nod to the Serenity prayer, recited at the end of Alcoholics Anonymous meetings. The date of the article is because it's well before the launch of ChatGPT at the end of 2022.

About a year and a half later, we reported that Serenity OS turns five and emits first offspring, Ladybird. Both the OS and the browser were still hand-coded, but now the browser could be compiled and run on other OSes. That freed it up to call upon external libraries which didn't exist for SerenityOS.

Earlier this year, we wrote Ladybird flutters toward Rust with a little help from AI. At one point, developer Andreas Kling used Apple's Swift language, but this year, he changed course and adopted Rust instead, using LLM tools to convert some existing code. Some will dismiss Ladybird because of this, but as our first coverage shows, the browser and its original host OS were established projects before the current wave of AI-assisted development.

Kling does use LLMs, but Ladybird is not some sloppy vibe-coded effort. The macOS download is 68.4 MB in size, which in 2026 is remarkably small. The Flatpak is larger – about 111 MB – but it also pulls in some KDE dependencies which increase its size.

We tested it on Pop!_OS. It handles sites such as The Register and Hacker News and everything else we tried perfectly, and took just 6 percent of our Dell XPS13's CPU to play full-screen HD video from YouTube smoothly. In our short testing, we saw no crashes, hesitation, or any other problems at all.

The developers nevertheless warn that the alpha can crash, some websites will not work, and they make no security guarantees at this stage.

The use of LLMs will put some people off. However, this is not the only controversial thing about the project. As we have noted in our previous coverage, Ladybird belongs to the same political wing of the FOSS movement as Omarchy, XLibre, and other right-wing projects. If the LLM use doesn't put you off, the political views may. On the other hand, as we've seen from our earlier coverage of Omarchy and XLibre, the same factors also attract others.

The modern Web is an entire complex compute platform in its own right, and currently, only three tools support it – and two of those are interrelated. The dominant engines are Google's Blink, used by Chrome and other Chromium browsers; Apple's WebKit, used by Safari; and Mozilla's Gecko, used by Firefox. Blink was forked from WebKit.

Some day, when the Servo project matures some more, it may be another. Even so, today, the first preliminary release of Ladybird means that there are now four competitive modern browser engines. That's a significant step. ®
articles.summary: The independent Ladybird web browser has reached an important milestone: an alpha test version. What's more, it works well. These may not be the criteria by which some will judge it, though.

Ford unveils the GT41 as it hopes to win Le Mans again
articles.text:
Sixty years ago, after two failed attempts, Ford won the 24 Hours of Le Mans with its GT40 race car. In the years since, the Blue Oval has been back to France more than a few times, with varying success. It could never replicate the GT40’s success winning overall, but it celebrated the 40th anniversary with a class win. Now it wants another shot at the really big trophy, and it debuted the car during the Detroit Lions-Chicago Bears football game today: meet the GT41.

“Revealing the Ford GT41 is a significant moment for everyone involved in this program,” said Dan Sayers, manager of Ford Racing’s Hypercar program. “It's the result of an enormous amount of work across our engineering, design, and development teams and an important milestone on our journey towards 2027. We know the scale of the challenge ahead—the level of competition in Hypercar is incredibly high, and there are no shortcuts to success. Our focus has been on building the right foundations, bringing together the right people and making sure we learn as much as possible from every stage of development.”

The video was directed by Zack Snyder and features Matt Damon’s voice-over.

Like many other entrants in the World Endurance Championship’s Hypercar class, Ford has chosen the rear-wheel-drive LMDh technical approach rather than building the GT41 entirely from scratch, as Ferrari and Aston Martin do with their cars. LMDh cars start with one of four approved carbon fiber chassis—in this case, Ford is working with Oreca, which has also partnered with Genesis and Acura.

articles.title: ASI hands over 12th-century bronze idol, 2 other repatriated antiquities to Tamil Nadu Police
articles.text:
ASI hands over 12th-century bronze idol, 2 other repatriated antiquities to Tamil Nadu Police
ASI DG Yadubir Singh Rawat handed Somaskanda, Saint Sundarar with Paravai Nachiyar and Saint Kannappa Nayanar to the Idol Wing CID at Dharohar Bhawan
Three repatriated antiquities, including a 12th-century Chola-period bronze idol, were on Thursday handed over by the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) to the Tamil Nadu Police at a function held at the ASI headquarters here, marking a "significant step" towards the recovery and restitution of India's cultural heritage, officials said.
The antiquities comprise two bronze idols repatriated from the Smithsonian Museum in the US and one from The Hague in the Netherlands. They were formally handed over to the respective police officers, the ASI said.
Also read: BJP office-bearer chants ‘kamal khila de’ at Taj Mahal, Archaeological Survey of India files plaint
The antiquities include Somaskanda (Lord Shiva and Uma), a 12th-century Chola-period bronze idol photographed in 1959 at the Siva Temple, Sri Visvanatha in Alattur, Mannargudi Taluk, Thanjavur district of Tamil Nadu. It was repatriated from the Smithsonian Museum, the ministry said.
Another antiquity, Saint Sundarar with Paravai Nachiyar, is a 16th-century bronze idol belonging to the Vijayanagara period. It was photographed in 1956 at the Shiva Temple, Sri Narisvara in Viracholapuram, Kallakurichi Taluk, Tamil Nadu, and was also repatriated from the Smithsonian Museum, it said in a statement.
The third antiquity, Saint Kannappa Nayanar, is a Chola-period bronze idol from Arulmigu Agneeswarasamy Temple in Thirupugalur, Nagapattinam district in Tamil Nadu.
It depicts the Shaivite saint in a 'tribhanga' standing posture, with his right hand raised towards his eye. The idol was repatriated from The Hague, the ASI said.
"In a significant step towards the recovery and restitution of India's cultural heritage, the Archaeological Survey of India today handed over the three repatriated antiquities to the Idol Wing CID, Tamil Nadu Police, at Dharohar Bhawan, New Delhi," it said.

articles.title: Tech's outage problem needs maintenance, not conspiracy theories
articles.text:
Years of technical debt, increasingly complex systems, and underinvestment in IT operations have left organizations vulnerable to major outages, according to Forrester.

The analyst pointed to a seven-day stretch in November when failures disrupted Microsoft 365, US air traffic control, banking, and other critical services.

The coinciding outages provoked "a slew of conspiracy theories about cyberattacks and AI," Forrester said.

"The real culprit is tragically mundane: the culmination of decades of technical debt, the frenetic buildout of massively complex and highly interdependent systems, the concentration of risk, and the underinvestment in advanced operations."

Forrester urged technology suppliers and in-house IT teams to prioritize resilience as their systems grow more complex. Otherwise, "the tech estate will collapse like a house of cards, taking down consumer and business trust with it."

Earlier this month, Microsoft was left struggling to restore many of its cloud services after a core process running on some servers became "overwhelmed" and its attempts to fix the problem failed. Some of its services did not recover for another 24 hours.

In October, Google Cloud blamed a "power event" for taking down multiple online products for customers in Western Europe. Affected services included BigQuery Data Transfer Service, Cloud Filestore, Cloud Run, Google App Engine, and Google Kubernetes Engine.

In October last year, a major outage impacted Amazon Web Services (AWS), with even Amazon's own web page reported to be offline and dozens of other online services and websites affected.

Aviation and banking were also hit this month. A communications outage triggered a nationwide ground stop in the US on November 13, while incidents involving JPMorgan Chase, United Airlines, Apple, Workday, Gmail, and other services added to the sense of widespread instability.

"Claims that these were all part of one connected cyberattack or conspiracy are highly unlikely. The real story is much more mundane," the report said.

Forrester argued that organizations have prioritized visible improvements over repairs to the underlying technology.

"Modernization investments have favored visible change over structural renewal," wrote report authors Lauren Nelson and Mark Moccia. "Organizations routinely fund new customer experiences, cloud migrations, platform consolidation, and AI initiatives because leaders can connect them to growth or productivity.

"They are less enthusiastic about updating core systems, simplifying architectures, retiring obsolete components, and eliminating fragile interfaces. The result is a modern front end resting on an aging, brittle, and increasingly interconnected estate."

Forrester's recommendations are to map dependencies, test failures and recovery under realistic conditions, and use incidents and near misses to identify weaknesses before they cause another outage. ®

articles.title: Driven out of forests, 56 displaced elephants run into politics in Karnataka
articles.text:
Arun Dev is an Assistant Editor with the Karnataka bureau of Hindustan Times. A journalist for over 10 years, he has written extensively on crime and politics.
Driven out of forests, 56 displaced elephants run into politics in Karnataka
Karnataka’s plan to move 56 elephants from Hassan’s coffee estates to Bhadra has stalled after protests by legislators and residents in Chikkamagaluru.
The movement of 56 elephants out of Hassan’s coffee estates in Karnataka has run into a political roadblock, with the forest department temporarily suspending the operation after protests by legislators and residents in neighbouring Chikkamagaluru.
The herd, meanwhile, has scattered across three districts, with 39 elephants in Mudigere, 13 back in Belur and four tuskers moving towards Kodagu as of November 26. For the elephants, finding a safe home is proving almost as difficult as escaping one: forests are fragmented by plantations, roads and fences, while the prospect of moving them elsewhere has run into resistance from communities worried about inheriting the conflict.
The operation, launched after two people were killed in elephant attacks in Belur, began on November 21, following the capture of two tuskers on November 18 and 19. One was shifted to the Mathigodu elephant camp in Nagarahole Tiger Reserve, while the other was released into the wild in Bandipur after being fitted with a radio collar. The forest department then began guiding the remaining 56 elephants from Belur towards the Bhadra forests.
Although the operation has been suspended, officials are continuing to monitor the herd and guide the elephants in Mudigere towards the Tatakola forest area, which adjoins reserve forests. Forest minister Ramalinga Reddy is scheduled to meet legislators from the affected districts on November 30 to discuss the issue.
The dispute has raised a difficult question: moving elephants away from one set of villages may simply shift the risk to another, particularly as the habitats and traditional routes connecting forests become increasingly fragmented.
Political resistance across districts
Hassan district in-charge minister K M Shivalinge Gowda has defended the operation, arguing that Belur has barely 100 acres of forest and cannot provide adequate habitat for the elephants.
However, Congress MLAs Nayana Motamma, T D Rajegowda and H D Thammaiah have opposed moving the herd towards Chikkamagaluru, which also faces frequent human-elephant conflict.
Motamma, who represents Mudigere, submitted her resignation to the Assembly speaker on November 23, protesting against the movement of elephants into her constituency without consulting local elected representatives. She withdrew it after chief minister D K Shivakumar and senior Congress leaders intervened, but continued to demand assurances on public safety.
“I have to answer the people who elected me. I am not answerable merely to the government. If we cannot protect the people who elected us, what is the purpose of holding public office?” she said.
Reddy, meanwhile, said elephants belonged in forests rather than coffee estates and cautioned legislators against politicising the issue.
“These elephants belong to the forest and not to the coffee estates. Do not indulge in politics,” he said.
Fences, roads and shrinking habitats
Research from the Hassan landscape helps explain why moving elephants from one area to another may offer only temporary relief.
A study published in August in the Journal of Wildlife Science, titled Navigating the coffee fields: elephants’ use of habitat mosaics and the impacts of barriers on their spatial use of villages in a fragmented landscape of South India, examined elephant movement across 466 villages spread over approximately 1,180 sq km between 2023 and 2025.
Researchers from the Nature Conservation Foundation mapped 277 solar-powered fences erected around coffee plantations between 2010 and 2025. Together, these fences stretched 382 km and covered approximately 32 sq km, nearly 5% of the study area.
Nearly 20% of the identified refuge habitat fragments shared a boundary with a solar fence, while another 30% had fences within 300 metres.
“The proximity of fences to habitat refugia limited elephants’ access to resources, pushing them into new areas,” the researchers found.
The study also identified the expansion of National Highway 75 from two lanes to four as a barrier to elephant movement. Elephant activity hotspots recorded on both sides of the highway in 2023 shifted predominantly to its northern side in 2024 and remained concentrated there in 2025. The researchers linked the shift to the highway expansion, completed in 2023.
They recommended protecting refuge habitats, redesigning fences to allow elephant movement, discouraging new fencing near natural forests and constructing highway overpasses or underpasses at critical crossing points.
Corridors exist, connectivity doesn’t
Karnataka has nine identified elephant corridors, but the Union government had reported securing only two through private land purchases, according to a Rajya Sabha reply in March 2023.
The state acquired 25.37 acres for the Edayahalli-Doddasampige corridor in 2017 and another 16.30 acres at Muddahalli for the Chamarajanagar-Talamalai corridor in 2021-22.
The Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26 estimated the state’s elephant population at 6,395, based on the 2023 assessment. It also reported that the state had installed 428 km of railway barricades, 1,360.87 km of solar fencing and 1,775.41 km of elephant-proof trenches to reduce human-elephant conflict.
While these barriers can protect farms and settlements, their placement can also restrict elephants’ access to habitats and traditional movement routes.
Joseph Hoover, president of the United Conservation Movement and a former member of the Karnataka State Wildlife Board, said the conflict was being viewed too narrowly.
“We are blaming elephants for a crisis largely created by human intervention. Their habitats have been fragmented, food sources depleted and traditional corridors blocked. When elephants are forced out of forests into agricultural land, we cannot treat them as the problem. We have to address what drove them there,” he said.
“Capturing elephants and driving them back into forests will only provide temporary relief. Unless we restore habitats and protect corridors, we will continue to see more human deaths and more elephant deaths,” he added.
The human cost of conflict
For farmers in Hassan, the conflict has also meant repeated crop losses. Union government data show that the district recorded 4,285 cases of crop damage by elephants in 2022-23, for which ₹2.97 crore was paid in compensation.
The number of cases fell to 3,641 in 2023-24, but compensation rose to ₹4.07 crore. In 2024-25, the district recorded 3,015 cases, with ₹3.80 crore paid in compensation.
The same data recorded 24 human deaths in elephant attacks in Hassan between 2020-21 and 2024-25.
For the forest department, the immediate challenge is to manage the 56 elephants dispersed across Belur, Mudigere and towards Kodagu without exposing more communities to danger.
The November 30 meeting may resolve the immediate political dispute, but not the underlying conflict. Driven out of one landscape because of the threat they pose to people, the elephants face resistance in another. Shrinking habitats, plantations, roads and fences lie at the heart of the problem. Relocating the herd may shift the conflict, but will not address its causes.

Kept in paying guest (PG) accommodations, allegedly served substandard food and subjected to physical assault if they refused to work, the foreign nationals were forced to follow written scripts to cheat unsuspecting people in their own countries through fraudulent investment platforms, police said.
Also read: CBI nabs Hisar man for ‘cyber slavery’, trafficking of Indians to Southeast Asia
In a major crackdown in southwest Delhi's Dwarka on an alleged international human trafficking and cyber fraud network, the Crime Branch of the Delhi Police has rescued 164 foreign nationals, including 92 Indonesians and 72 Malaysians, from premises allegedly being used to operate the racket. A 25-year-old Malaysian national, identified as Tan Guan Wei, has been arrested in connection with the case.
According to police, the network specifically targeted people in Indonesia and Malaysia by offering them employment opportunities in India, promising attractive salaries and better career prospects. However, their ordeal allegedly began soon after they landed in the country.
Their passports were taken away upon arrival, leaving them without control over their identity documents and restricting their ability to leave, police said. They were subsequently shifted to PG accommodations and allegedly forced to work as cyber slaves.
Those who resisted or refused to participate in the fraudulent activities were allegedly thrashed by members of the network to ensure compliance, a senior police officer said, adding that so far they have learned that around two people were thrashed.
The living conditions at the accommodations were also allegedly poor, with the foreign nationals being provided substandard food. Despite a fleet of around 40 cabs being used to ferry them between the PG accommodations and the cyber fraud call centre, they were not allowed to venture out independently or move around as they wished, the officer said.

"The cabs were allegedly deployed to transport them to the call centre and bring them back to their accommodations, ensuring that their movement remained under the control of the handlers," the officer said.
The foreign nationals were not merely made to operate computers and mobile phones but were allegedly trained to execute a specific pattern of cyber fraud. They were provided written scripts containing conversations that they had to follow while approaching prospective victims.
The targets were primarily people in Malaysia and Indonesia. The operators allegedly created fictitious female identities and social media profiles to establish contact with unsuspecting individuals.

"Using these profiles, the foreign nationals were instructed to initiate conversations, develop online relationships and gradually gain the confidence of their targets. Once trust was established, the victims were persuaded to invest money through fraudulent trading and investment platforms," the officer added.
The syndicate allegedly used websites and APK-based applications to lure people with promises of high returns. The victims were made to believe that they were investing in legitimate financial opportunities, while the money was allegedly siphoned off through the fraudulent network.
"We got to know about the fraud after the crime branch received an email alert about the alleged cyber slavery racket around a week ago, following which its officers began developing intelligence about the network," the officer said.
Initial information suggested that around 60 to 70 foreign nationals were being held and forced to work in the cyber fraud operation. However, when the police team conducted the operation at the suspected premises, the actual number turned out to be significantly higher. The operation led to the rescue of 164 foreign nationals, exposing the scale of the alleged racket.
The police are now investigating how the foreign nationals were recruited, who facilitated their travel to India, and how their passports were taken away. "During the entire investigation, two names -- Sunil Kumar and Sushil Bhati -- cropped up. Bhati used to arrange the PG accommodations and transportation facilities. Both are absconding, both will be arrested soon," the officer said.
Certain bank accounts allegedly maintained by Kumar and Bhati have been identified as being used to meet rental and other operational expenses of the network. The financial trail is being examined to establish the flow of money, identify the beneficiaries and trace the proceeds generated through the alleged cyber fraud. The arrested Malaysian national, Tan Guan Wei, a resident of Negeri Sembilan, is being questioned about his alleged role in the network, his association with other members and the extent of his involvement in operating the fraudulent platforms.
The police have seized a substantial digital infrastructure allegedly used to run the operation. The recoveries include 355 mobile phones, 168 desktop computers, 26 laptops, 53 SIM cards and 174 passports. Of the 355 mobile phones, 335 were old or used handsets, and 20 were new phones in sealed packaging. The 53 SIM cards include 31 international and 22 Indian connections. The recovered passports comprise 95 Indonesian and 79 Malaysian documents.
Servers and other electronic material have also been seized. Investigators are examining the devices to identify the victims, establish the communication channels used by the syndicate and trace financial transactions linked to the fraudulent platforms.

articles.text:
Abhijeet Dipke launches nationwide ‘Save Democracy’ movement at Constitution Day rally in Nagpur
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke announced a nationwide campaign at a Nagpur rally, while actor Prakash Raj backed calls to protect democracy and constitutional rights.
Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke on Thursday announced a nationwide movement to “Save Democracy and Save Constitution”, urging citizens to unite against what he alleged were threats to democratic rights, electoral freedoms and constitutional values. Actor Prakash Raj, who joined a rally in Nagpur to mark Constitution Day, also called for greater protection of dissent and freedom of expression.
Addressing the gathering in Nagpur on Thursday evening, Dipke urged people to uphold constitutional values, protect democracy and follow the ideals of Babasaheb Ambedkar, the chief architect of the Constitution. Appealing to young people to take the lead, he raised concerns about electoral processes, social media moderation and the protection of democratic safeguards.
Speaking in Hindi and Marathi, Dipke said the earlier protest at Jantar Mantar had given young people a platform to voice their concerns. “You have power. We have the Constitution,” he said, questioning the government over alleged electoral irregularities, including discrepancies in vote counts during the last hour of polling and the deletion of names from voter lists.
He also questioned the Maharashtra government’s reported move to overturn the outcome of the Gokul dairy election through an ordinance, asking what such interventions could mean for larger electoral contests.
Referring to what he described as a lookout notice issued by Mumbai police, Dipke said he was in Nagpur and would continue protesting. He urged supporters to remain united and continue peaceful demonstrations even if they were detained.
Dipke also called for 50% representation for women in cabinets and in the distribution of election tickets by political parties. Citing Ambedkar’s work on women’s rights and labour protections, he said his legacy should be recognised across communities.
He said the Constitution had enabled people from humble backgrounds to reach the highest public offices, citing Prime Minister Narendra Modi as an example. Recalling a visit to the tribal district of Gadchiroli, Dipke alleged that he had seen classrooms without benches and bathing facilities for tribal girls without roofs or doors. He questioned how long children in such schools would have to wait for basic infrastructure.
Dipke, who had been in Nagpur since Wednesday to organise the rally, described Constitution Day as a significant occasion and urged citizens to defend democratic and voting rights.
Earlier in the day, Dipke paid floral tributes to Ambedkar at Nagpur’s historic Deekshabhoomi, where the latter and his followers embraced Buddhism in 1956, underscoring the symbolic significance of the location for the campaign.
Prakash Raj, meanwhile, criticised the government over what he alleged were attempts to silence dissent, warning that suppressing the voices of students and young people would only make them louder.
He said protecting the rights and freedoms guaranteed by the Constitution was a collective responsibility and called on citizens to come together to defend democratic freedoms. He alleged that young people raising questions about education, healthcare and employment were increasingly being silenced instead of receiving answers from the government.
“Attempts to suppress voices will only make them louder,” Raj said, stressing that young people’s freedom of expression must be respected and their questions addressed.
He also expressed concern over reports of citizens being prevented from travelling abroad even after boarding flights. Referring to a recent case involving YouTuber Dhruv Rathee, Raj questioned the restrictions on citizens’ freedoms and alleged that people carrying the national flag were also being jailed.
Raj said the campaign aimed to remove the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) from power, adding that any political party taking steps against the Constitution would face opposition. He maintained that the movement was not about conventional politics but about defending constitutional values and democratic rights.
On Jantar Mantar being denied as a protest site, Raj said that protest spaces would emerge across the country, including in neighbourhoods and on streets.
Dipke also raised concerns about the visibility of political content on social media platforms. He alleged that posts about Prime Minister Narendra Modi were being promoted, while content critical of other political leaders and parties was being restricted. He alleged that more than 50 lakh Instagram posts had been taken down between January and June, although the figure and his allegation of political bias in content moderation have not been independently verified.
Dipke further alleged that the government had prevented 27-year-old CJP co-convenor Saurav Das from travelling to the London School of Economics and Oxford University out of “jealousy” over invitations he had received from the institutions.
Dipke said CJP co-convenors Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, along with him, had been invited to the UK. They had decided that Das would travel to London, while he and Ranka would visit parts of Maharashtra to assess drought conditions. However, Das was stopped at the airport, he alleged.
“The move stemmed from jealousy,” Dipke added.
He said the three had been invited to speak about how the Jantar Mantar protest, guided by the ideals of Ambedkar and Mahatma Gandhi, had garnered widespread support. “But this individual is a narcissist, he wants not just the country, but the entire world to revolve around him. He believes that he alone should travel across the world,” he added.
Das approached the Delhi high court on Wednesday challenging the action. The Ministry of External Affairs, meanwhile, said he had been issued a show-cause notice seeking an explanation for discrepancies concerning his place of birth in his passport..

articles.title: UK privacy watchdog faces probe into its workplace culture
articles.text:
Britain's privacy watchdog is getting a taste of its own medicine, with an independent review set to examine the culture, governance, and accountability surrounding the events that led to former Information Commissioner John Edwards' resignation.

Karon Monaghan KC will examine whether the regulator's culture and governance allowed problems to develop or made concerns harder to raise.

Edwards quit in June after an independent workplace investigation found there was a "case to answer" over his behavior and that his conduct fell short of what was expected of a public official. He disagreed with some of its findings, but ultimately conceded that he had shown "poor judgment."

That investigation, however, focused on Edwards alone. According to the terms of reference published on Thursday, it "did not consider the wider conditions in which that conduct occurred, and it was not designed to."

The new review will cast a wider net. Monaghan wants to know whether staff could call out bad behavior further up the food chain, and what awaited those who tried.

It will also poke around the regulator's leadership and governance arrangements and its relationship with its sponsoring government department, including whether there were adequate ways for concerns to be escalated and those at the top to be challenged.

Current and former staff can give evidence confidentially and voluntarily, while Monaghan will be given access to relevant documents and existing material, including staff surveys and data on bullying, harassment and discrimination.

The ICO has confirmed it won't use confidentiality clauses in settlement agreements to prevent people from contributing to the review.

Monaghan decides which witnesses and documents are relevant, rather than the ICO or DCMS. Access remains subject to legal restrictions, and she must be told when material is withheld and why. She can speak to whoever she thinks is relevant and ask for the complaints, correspondence, and other paperwork she needs.

And if that leads her somewhere unexpected, she can ask to widen the investigation. DCMS can refuse, but it won't be able to quietly brush the request aside, and any decision not to expand the scope has to make it into the final report.

The review won't reopen the investigation into Edwards, make findings about the conduct of named individuals, or delve into the merits of the regulator's enforcement decisions.

Its arrival comes amid a broader shake-up at Britain's data watchdog. The old Information Commissioner's Office was formally replaced by the Information Commission on September 30, bringing with it a new board-led governance model.

The government first promised the wider review in July, shortly after Edwards' departure, but it didn't appoint its reviewer or nail down the terms until late November.

"We need to understand what is working, where things are falling short and, crucially, what needs to change," said DCMS Secretary Lisa Nandy.

The watchdog won't have to wait long for its report card. Monaghan is expected to deliver her findings in the first quarter of 2027, after which they will be published and handed to Parliament. ®

Understanding the debate over delimitation and women’s quota as Centre proposes special Parliament sitting
The 131st constitution amendment bill sought to raise the Lok Sabha ceiling to 850 and implement 33% reservation for women in time for the 2029 polls.
The government’s decision to propose a special sitting of Parliament has brought back the focus on a Constitution Amendment Bill to expand the size of the Lok Sabha and fast-track 33% reservation for women.
In April, the bill failed to garner the required two-thirds majority in the Lok Sabha. It was the first time a constitutional amendment brought by the government had been defeated since the National Democratic Alliance (NDA) came to power in 2014.
Subsequently, the government withdrew two other linked bills. One mandated delimitation on the basis of the latest available census, effectively the 2011 one. The other implemented the changes in union territories.
Also Read | Parliament session reconvened: How women’s reservation bill failed in April
Constitution amendment bills can be introduced in either House of Parliament. While motions for introduction of such bills are adopted by simple majority , a majority of the total membership of the House and a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting is required for adoption of effective clauses and motions for consideration and passing of these bills.
While proposing a special sitting of Parliament on Thursday, the government did not mention the agenda. But speculation has been rife that a special sitting could be arranged to push through the 131st constitution amendment bill and the delimitation bill.
What fuelled the buzz was the fact that the government did not prorogue the Monsoon Session, which was adjourned sine die on August 13.
Govt vs Opposition
The 131st constitution amendment bill sought to raise the Lok Sabha ceiling to 850 and implement 33% reservation for women in time for the 2029 polls. It lost the Parliament test in the face of a united Opposition, which did not waver despite a dramatic last-minute offer by Union home minister Amit Shah to incorporate a 50% proportional rise for all states into the bill.
While the ruling side hit the streets in protest against the bill’s defeat, the Opposition said it favoured women’s reservation but opposed delimitation, and questioned the government’s timing and intent.
Reserving a third of seats in legislative assemblies and the Lok Sabha has been debated since the Constituent Assembly, which rejected the idea. Previous attempts to pass the bill were repeatedly thwarted in the 1990s and 2000s as regional parties opposed the move. In 2010, the bill passed the Rajya Sabha but was stalled in the Lok Sabha. Finally, in 2023, the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam passed the Parliament test, mandating that 33% reservation for women will be rolled out based on a fresh census and delimitation.
Also Read | Ministers, lawmakers put travel plans on hold amid uncertainty surrounding Parliament session
To be sure, the 2023 women’s reservation act still stands. It came into force in April this year.
In the budget session, the government introduced three bills aimed at delinking the women’s quota from the next census and tying it instead to a delimitation based on the 2011 census. The government’s legislative push involved raising the cap on seats in the Lok Sabha, with the allocation of seats to states, the reserved constituencies and their boundaries being defined by a delimitation commission on the basis of the latest census, which would mean the 2011 one in this case.
North-South debate
The Opposition and leaders of southern states flagged concerns over the exercise, with critics calling it a flawed, unconstitutional and anti-federal exercise.
One of the biggest points of contention was a North vs South divide. A section of critics argue that North India could gain more seats in proportion to its population, while South India, which contributes around 30–31% of the GDP, could lose out because of the population factor. Southern states have time and again flagged that population alone shouldn’t be the criterion for such revisions or additions. The government countered that under a uniform 50% increase, the southern states’ share of Lok Sabha seats would rise slightly, from 23.76% to 23.87%. Critics pointed out that the bill itself did not guarantee that formula.

He has 10 years of experience writing for print and digital platforms and has worked at The New York Times, NDTV and The Indian Express in the past. He specialises in longform reportage at the intersections of politics, crime, social commentary and environment.
Wayanad set to become India’s first e-waste-free district after 102 tonnes collected
Kerala’s Wayanad collected 102.85 tonnes of discarded electronics in a three-month drive and is set to be declared India’s first e-waste-free district on Friday.
Kerala’s Wayanad is set to become India’s first district free of electronic waste (e-waste), with chief minister VD Satheesan scheduled to make the formal announcement on Friday after a three-month campaign collected more than 102 tonnes of discarded electronic items for scientific disposal, officials said.
The roadmap for an ‘e-waste-free, climate-resilient district’ was drawn up three months ago and implemented in three phases across Wayanad’s 23 grama panchayats and three municipalities, said T Siddique, minister for agriculture and Wayanad district-in-charge.
“A total of 102.85 metric tonnes of e-waste was collected door-to-door from various sources and handed over to Clean Kerala Company for scientific management and disposal. This was possible because of the active involvement of the general public, government officials, tourist destinations, traders, restaurant owners and educational institution in-charges. As we are a hill district facing the effects of climate change and targeting revenue through tourism, this initiative gives us a lot of confidence,” Siddique said. He stressed the need to sustain the e-waste-free status in the coming years.
The waste collected included discarded computers, television sets, refrigerators, batteries, circuit boards, electronic components and cables.
“E-waste is extremely harmful to soil, water and our general environment. It contains heavy metals like lead, mercury, cadmium etc which can leach into soil or groundwater when burned or dumped. Documented health effects include neurological illnesses, cancers and respiratory disorders,” the minister said.
Officials said the three-month campaign was carried out in three phases. In the first, e-waste was collected from government offices in coordination with Clean Kerala Company.
The second phase involved door-to-door collection from households and private institutions by the Haritha Karma Sena, the sanitation workers’ unit of the local self-government department. Collection points were also set up across panchayats and municipalities.
In the final phase, households and institutions missed during the earlier rounds were covered through ward-level collection drives.
The minister’s office said in a statement that the collaborative effort “brought key stakeholders through consultations” and involved “regular follow-up and review meetings” to monitor progress.
Such environmental initiatives are particularly important for Wayanad, which has faced ecological disasters linked to deforestation, large-scale infrastructure development and the long-term effects of climate change.
In 2024, the district witnessed one of Kerala’s deadliest landslides in Meppadi village, killing more than 400 people and displacing 10,000.

Odisha women cops to get 12 days’ menstrual leave, exemption from strenuous duties if pregnant
Odisha Police has directed districts to grant women personnel 12 days of additional casual leave annually for menstrual discomfort and ease duties for pregnant and lactating staff.
Bhubaneswar The Odisha Police has advised district superintendents of police (SPs) to exempt pregnant and lactating women personnel, as far as practicable, from night duties and strenuous assignments, and ensure 12 days of additional casual leave annually for women to manage menstrual discomfort.
In a letter issued to district SPs on Wednesday, the Crime Against Women and Children (CAW & CW) Wing of the Odisha Police said pregnant and lactating personnel should be exempted from strenuous physical duties involving prolonged standing, physical exertion and law-and-order deployments.
Women experiencing severe menstrual discomfort may be assigned less strenuous duties, such as control room responsibilities, instead of physically demanding field assignments, wherever operational requirements permit, it said.
Citing the disproportionate burden of household and caregiving responsibilities on women, alongside the demanding nature of police service, including round-the-clock duties, night deployments, stressful working conditions and time-bound investigations, the wing said the combined burden of professional and domestic responsibilities adversely affected the mental health and overall well-being of women police personnel. It said this made it imperative to create a supportive and gender-responsive working environment.
The wing also noted that women police personnel in some districts were not being allowed to avail themselves of leave and directed all authorities to ensure that eligible personnel received the benefit upon application.
Citing a March 12, 2024, order of the state finance department sanctioning 12 days of additional casual leave annually for women government employees, the letter said women police personnel should be granted one day of additional leave every month to address physical discomfort during menstruation.
It also called for reasonable breaks and flexibility in duty timings for pregnant and lactating women to facilitate breastfeeding and childcare requirements, citing provisions of the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961.
“Nursing breaks should be allowed to enable mothers to attend to their infants. District SPs should sympathetically consider requests for additional leave supported by genuine grounds and medical certificates, particularly when women require more time for post-delivery recovery, breastfeeding or newborn care,” the letter said.
To address deployment-related grievances, district SPs have been asked to attach a woman sub-inspector, assistant sub-inspector or havildar to the Force Section in each Reserve Office. The designated officer will facilitate the appropriate deployment of women havildars and constables and escalate genuine grievances to the Reserve Inspector and district SP.
The directive also mandates the appointment of a woman officer of the rank of deputy superintendent of police (DSP) or additional SP as a well-being officer in every district. The officer will serve as a point of contact for women personnel and facilitate grievance redressal.
Besides ensuring separate, clean and hygienic toilets, SPs have been asked to provide separate changing rooms at all duty posts and restore women’s rest rooms that have been diverted for other purposes.
The directive also calls for regular gender-sensitivity training for supervisory officers, timely disposal of sexual harassment complaints under the 2013 law, and access to professional counsellors and psychologists for personnel facing mental health challenges.
District SPs have further been directed to earmark at least 15 minutes during monthly ‘Alochana Sabha’ meetings exclusively for interactions with women police personnel to discuss their gender-specific concerns and grievances.

Founded in March 2026 with teams in Paris and Brittany, Arsenals raised initial funding in two weeks and built its first autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) prototype in five weeks at its Brittany workshop. The company currently employs more than 20 people and aims to grow to 150 within a year.

Designated “The Harpoon” by the company, the vehicle is built around a common platform with plug-and-play payload modularity, including seeker heads, warheads, and sensors. According to Allanot, the system prioritizes speed, endurance, communications, and autonomous navigation in post-GNSS environments, allowing a single fleet to carry out intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR), target acquisition, decoy, and strike missions.

Arsenals is positioning the platform as an attritable force multiplier designed to create tactical depth ahead of legacy naval fleets, absorbing threats and saturating contested waters while also serving peacetime training roles. To enable mass replenishment, the company is targeting a manufacturing takt time of one hour, allowing a stockpile of 100 vehicles to be produced in 100 hours. In lean manufacturing, takt time (from Taktzeit, literally “beat time” in German) defines the required production cadence, or the maximum time allowed to complete a single unit in order to meet demand.

While the exact technology readiness level remains confidential, Allanot confirmed that demonstrations and testing are underway with the French armed forces ahead of a planned product launch next year. Asked during the interview whether Arsenals sees itself as a French counterpart to Anduril, Allanot welcomed the comparison: “We are ready to race against Anduril. So Palmer, if you want to do an underwater race, let’s do it.”

articles.title: 'Significant number of customer records' pwned in Flight Centre Travel Group breach
articles.text:
Travel giant Flight Centre Travel Group (FLT) says "a significant number of customer records" may have been accessed by "unknown persons" following a cyberattack.

The Brisbane-headquartered company said the incident affected a third-party accommodation booking system used by Flight Centre, Travel Associates, Cruiseabout, and some independent travel agents.

Its disclosure [PDF], filed with the Australian Securities Exchange today, added that it was aware that records were accessed, but cannot definitively say how many were exfiltrated.

Flight Centre is working with the supplier and incident response specialist Mandiant to establish the scope of the incident.

An initial review suggests most accessed records contained only customer names, some with basic travel information. A "very small percentage" may also include birth dates, email addresses, limited passport details, phone numbers, or, in rare cases, health or mobility information.

Flight bookings and corporate travel use separate systems and are unaffected, the company said.

"FLT values customer privacy and data security," the company said in its disclosure. "The company understands that an incident like this can be unsettling for customers who may be affected, and we apologize for any concern this causes."

Investigations remain ongoing, but FLT has already contained the attack, rotated keys and credentials, and increased system monitoring, it said.

The company said it would contact affected customers directly. Its brands continue to operate normally, and travelers should proceed with their plans.

Customers should independently verify unexpected messages about their bookings before clicking links, opening attachments, or sharing personal information.

The attack on FLT follows others that have hit booking systems in the past year, including those on Booking.com and BWH Hotels.

More recently, another Australian business, RMS Cloud, which provides booking software to travel and leisure companies, also acknowledged a breach that led to WhatsApp scams in late October.

Numerous reports of travelers being targeted with messages that contained their names and booking details hit local news outlets at the time.

Customers were sent convincing messages seemingly from the hotels they had booked, and according to Australia's National Anti-Scam Centre, the scams appeared to be financially motivated.

Muhammad Yahya Patel, vCISO and cybersecurity advisor for EMEA at Huntress, said attackers targeting booking systems is a "familiar supply chain story" that has a greater impact than simple data theft.

Speaking generally about the risks of exposed travel records, Patel said: "Unlike a compromised email address or phone number, a passport can't be changed easily or quickly. For affected customers, the practical risk extends well beyond the immediate breach.

"Passport details combined with names, addresses, and travel history create a comprehensive identity profile that enables document fraud, identity theft, and targeted social engineering that could persist for years." ®

Rackspace pulls plug on Spot cloud service after security breach
articles.text:
Rackspace is shutting down its low-cost Spot cloud service after a security breach, giving customers two weeks' notice to move their workloads and retrieve their data.

In a notice posted on Tuesday, the cloud computing biz said its Rackspace Spot service will cease operations at 1700 Central Time (2300 UTC) on December 8. Any workloads still running at that point will be terminated, and customers will no longer be able to access their data.

"Following the recent security incident affecting Rackspace Spot, Rackspace has made the decision to wind down the service," the company said. "Spot customers are being notified with the wind-down timeline, instructions for retrieving their data and steps to secure their environments."

Customers will have to contend with the fallout from the breach while simultaneously trying to get their applications and data off the platform.

According to a customer notification seen by The Register, the attackers used leaked credentials to access parts of Rackspace Spot over a period of almost 22 hours on November 17. Rackspace only learned of the intrusion the following day, after a customer raised the alarm.

The intruders impersonated legitimate users, created pods in customer Kubernetes clusters, gained access to stored credentials known as Kubernetes Secrets, and listed nodes and storage volumes.

"With that access, they could have read any Secret in an affected user's clusters, and any Spot API token or refresh token that user held," Rackspace told customers.

Rackspace has since revoked the affected tokens and sessions, removed the pods planted by the intruders, and changed the affected platform and storage keys. Customers must also reissue API tokens, download new Kubernetes configuration files, and rotate credentials stored in their clusters, including database passwords and third-party API keys.

Sirish Raghuram, co-founder and chief growth officer of Platform9, which co-developed Spot with Rackspace, shed some light on the root cause in a November 20 GitHub post.

"An observability system was breached using a compromised credential," Raghuram wrote. "This was obviously a critical error on our part and we are very sorry we let this happen."

Raghuram said the incident necessitated significant changes to the underlying infrastructure clusters, prolonging the outage.

Spot's selling point was cheap compute. The service operated an auction-based pricing model, allowing customers to bid for cloud infrastructure at a fraction of the cost of conventional on-demand instances. Rackspace advertised savings of up to 90 percent for customers willing to tolerate interruptions to their workloads. A permanent interruption probably wasn't what they had in mind.

Rackspace hasn't explained why it chose closure over recovery, revealed how many customers were affected, or said whether it will offer migration extensions. It did not respond to The Register's questions. ®

Arunachal anti-dam activists Ebo Mili, Otul Jerang get bail in Pasighat violence case
Anti-dam activists Ebo Mili and Otul Jerang have been granted bail in the October 23 Pasighat violence case amid protests against Arunachal’s proposed Siang dam.
Prominent anti-dam activist Ebo Mili and youth leader Otul Jerang were among those granted bail by a court in Arunachal Pradesh’s East Siang district on Thursday in connection with the October 23 violence in Pasighat, amid continuing protests against the proposed 11,000-MW Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP).
The two activists, who have been leading protests against the proposed project, were arrested on October 24 after surrendering at a police station. East Siang superintendent of police Pankaj Lamba had said that 26 people, including five juveniles, were arrested in connection with the violence that erupted during the October 23 anti-SUMP bandh.
The arrests followed a 12-hour shutdown across Siang, Upper Siang and parts of East Siang districts, called by organisations demanding the release of activists detained during earlier demonstrations.
Tensions escalated after security personnel reportedly fired tear gas to disperse protesters near Geku. Four women were subsequently admitted to the local primary health centre, but police later clarified that all four were discharged after medical observation. The unrest subsequently spread to Pasighat, where an NHPC office was set ablaze, a police station was attacked and several vehicles were damaged.
The Adi Bane Kebang United (ABKU) and the Siang Indigenous Farmers’ Forum (SIFF) have been demanding the release of arrested protesters and the withdrawal of security forces from the Siang belt as preconditions for dialogue with the state government.
Despite repeated attempts to contact officials, the exact number of people released on bail and further details of the case could not be ascertained at the time of filing this report.
Meanwhile, opposition to mega hydropower projects has gathered momentum beyond Arunachal Pradesh, with anti-dam organisations from the state and neighbouring Assam joining hands to launch a coordinated mass movement.
Anti-Mega Dam People’s Forum spokesperson and retired Tinsukia College principal Rana Kumar Changmai announced plans to constitute mass struggle committees across Assam and convene a convention across the Northeast to consolidate opposition to large hydropower projects. The decision was announced at a press conference in Assam’s Dibrugarh on Wednesday, following a meeting of representatives from both states.
The forum also plans to approach opposition leaders in New Delhi to raise the issue in Parliament and mobilise international opposition to China’s proposed mega dam on the Yarlung Tsangpo river.
Representatives from Arunachal Pradesh reiterated their opposition to hydropower projects proposed on the Siang and Dibang rivers.
The SUMP has faced sustained resistance from sections of the indigenous Adi community over fears of large-scale displacement, submergence of ancestral land and environmental degradation.
Chief minister Pema Khandu had earlier maintained that the pre-feasibility study for SUMP did not constitute approval for the construction of the dam and reiterated the government’s willingness to engage with affected communities through dialogue.
Union home minister Amit Shah, during his recent visit to Arunachal Pradesh, also assured constructive dialogue with affected communities and promised a comprehensive rehabilitation and resettlement package.

articles.title: Wyoming uranium operation shuts down after cyberattack
articles.text:
Peninsula Energy has temporarily shut down its Wyoming uranium operation after a "cybersecurity incident" affected plant and wellfield control systems.

The Australian uranium producer said on Wednesday that it had activated its response procedures and brought in outside specialists following the attack on its US subsidiary, Strata Energy, which operates the Lance uranium project.

Peninsula Energy said it believes the attack is "confined to the plant and wellfield operating and control systems," and that back-office functions, such as payroll and other corporate systems, in both the US and Australia, remain unaffected.

"The company's immediate priorities have been to protect the safety of its employees, secure its operating systems, and work towards the restoration of operations in a safe and controlled manner," it said in an update to the Australian Securities Exchange.

The notification [PDF] went on to say that Peninsula Energy's investigations into the attack, including whether any data was compromised, remain ongoing.

Peninsula has not given a restart date and says it cannot yet assess the impact on its 2027 production guidance. Operations will remain suspended until recovery and safety checks are complete. "Peninsula will provide further updates to the market as material information becomes available," it said.

The disclosure of additional information came two days after Peninsula secured a short trading halt, which referenced a cybersecurity incident at its Wyoming site.

The November 23 filing [PDF] dated the incident to Friday evening in Western Australia. Wednesday's update clarified that Strata detected it on the morning of November 20, local US time.

Peninsula subsequently requested a voluntary suspension of trading until the earlier of November 30 or an announcement on restarting operations and any resulting change to production guidance.

Peninsula's Lance project is a uranium mining operation, extracting the element from underground deposits and turning it into uranium concentrate, aka yellowcake or U₃O₈.

Uranium concentrate is feedstock for nuclear fuel production, typically undergoing conversion, enrichment, and fabrication into uranium dioxide pellets before use in reactors.

The Lance central processing plant was constructed to produce a maximum of 2.0 million pounds (Mlb) of U₃O₈ annually, and is licensed for 3.0 Mlb.

Peninsula previously forecast production of 500,000 to 600,000 pounds in 2027, having withdrawn its 2026 guidance earlier this year following operational problems at Lance. It now says it will reassess the 2027 outlook once operations resume. ®

articles.title: Company was religious about backups but sinned by leaving them exposed
articles.text:
Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where we’re thankful every time someone leaves a password sticky note on a monitor or fails to delete a terminated employee’s admin account. But neither of those common occurrences is what we’ll be talking about today. Instead, our subject broke the number-one rule of backups: you gotta keep ’em separated.

Our story comes courtesy of Da Li, who serves as global alliance manager at Info2Soft, a company that provides data protection and recovery software. At one point, a partner called him into a case where a Chinese vehicle parts manufacturer fell victim to a ransomware gang. Unfortunately, its backup was compromised too.

The manufacturer had religiously backed up its manufacturing execution system (MES) and SAP orders, inventory, and finance systems every night. There was even a green dashboard that showed the backup process had succeeded, and someone checked that every morning.

However, one Friday evening, crims broke into the network and found out that the backup server was joined to the same Windows domain as the rest of the network. The hackers found a plaintext password for the backup service account in a maintenance script on a file share and discovered that someone had used the very same password for a domain admin account.

So the first thing the crooks did was delete every restore point on that backup server. Then they started encrypting the production servers to ransom them.

“Every backup job had succeeded for three years,” Li said. “The failure was that the thing meant to save them could be reached with the same keys as the thing being attacked.”

The results were devastating. With the MES and SAP data both gone, the plant couldn't schedule production, ship parts, or track them.

By the time Li was called in, the plant had already resolved its ransomware situation. We don’t know whether it paid or not. The manufacturer did ask Li and his company to make sure that this couldn’t happen again.

Li’s fix was not radical, but it was instructive. He made sure that the company now keeps its backup system outside the production domain, uses unique credentials, and requires MFA to reduce the risk of unauthorized access even if a password is compromised. He also made sure that the company keeps at least one offline backup and runs a test restore quarterly to ensure it’s prepared for emergencies.®
